questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: 1. Common law jurisdiction. 2. English-speaking country. 3. Small university. 4. Outside Europe.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I enjoyed it, but it was hard work! You should only choose this law school if you go on exchange for academic reasons because you have to study a lot, also during the weekends.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy! W&L was helpful. I emailed with them about everything, and they also sent a packet from the U.S. to my address in Denmark with relevant information (primarily for the VISA).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Just before I arrived, I got an email with information about the orientation week. During the first day of that week, I talked with Dean Mason, and I got an information packet with all relevant information. She was helpful and told me that I could always reach out to her. The same thing did Hunter Swanson who is the international coordinator (for law school and undergrad). He also held a meeting for the international law students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy! I used the Facebook group: "W&L House Exchange" and posted information about myself and my needs. 3 different students contacted me, and I chose to live with an American law student around 5 minutes from the school. I was lucky because I heard from many students how difficult it was to find housing in or near Lexington.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Choose a place in town or near law school. It is impossible to live elsewhere if you do not have a car.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As it is difficult to find housing in Lexington, and the demand is high, I think that W&L should offer on-campus housing for law exchange students. They do so for undergrad exchange students.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I just e-mailed with the law registar, and he sent a list of available courses that I could choose. I e-mailed back with my preferences, and then he fixed the registration. During the summer, I got my W&L e-mail, and then I was able to see my registrations on Workday (the app they use for course registration). Normally, the students register themselves, but the school does it for the exchange students which was very nice. But be aware that the American students register before the exchange students, so I could only choose between the less popular courses which was very annoying.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: See answer above.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: At first, I was not successful. Many of the courses I wanted were not available because they were already full. I only got 2 out of 4 courses. I was, however, lucky when I got there. One course got a free spot the day before we started, and I was able to get it. Thus I got 3 courses I wanted and ended up taking 1 that I did not prefer.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a drop/add policy the first two weeks. Check Workday just before start and then regularly afterwards to see if any new spots are offered because students drop the courses frequently in this period.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I learned a lot, but it was also a lot of hard work! It was way more than in Denmark, and the readings were 140 % more pages than it would have been with 30 ECTS in Copenhagen. You will get used to it, but you have to put a lot of effort into it, and it is not unusual to study during the weekends.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Law school is grad level in the U.S which is equivalent to MA.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: More readings. Your participation in class is part of your final grade. The professors check in the beginning of every class who is there and who is not. No fictive study cases which we have all the time in Copenhagen. The professors cold call, and if you are not prepared for class, they will ask you to leave. If you do not like speaking in class, this is not a place for you.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: 1. Poverty Law (3 credits = 7,5 ECTS). 2. Business Associations (4 credits = 10 ECTS). 3. National Security Law (2 credits = 5 ECTS). 4. Alternative Dispute Resolution (3 credits = 7,5 ECTS).

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend all of them. They were different in many ways, but they were all amazing. It was a great way to try different subjects and teaching methods. 1. BA was heavy, as it is a bar exam course. You had to make case briefs for every case (usually 5-8 cases per class), and it was a lot of work. However, I really ended up enjoying it. The professor was so good! It was a wonderful experience having her. 2. ADR was amazing. The professor had been living in France for many years, so the amount of readings were on European level = less than the other classes. We had role plays in almost every class, and I improved my speaking a lot in these classes. We did different mediations and negotiations as well as one big international arbitration mock case. 3. National Security Law was my favourite. It was due to the different subjects in class, as I have specialized in human rights law which was the core of the class because American national security law usually conflicts with human rights. I also got a really close relationship with the professor. He was very helpful, also outside class. His teaching method was primarily him speaking and then open discussions in class. We also had different guest lecturers such as a FBI agent and attorneys working with international espionage and counter-terrorism. It was incredible. The exam was tough because it was a research paper (25-30 pages) which was a lot of work for only 5 ECTS. 4. I also enjoyed Poverty Law. The professor was a legend at W&L, and it was her last class before retiring after almost 40 years of teaching at the school. The class was about welfare law and social security law in the U.S. It was amazing to learn about because it is in such contrast to the Danish welfare society. Nothing less than a good experience. I felt really proud of being Danish, and it was shocking to learn about the American society.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The utilities were higher than expected because of the energy prices and inflation. Buying groceries was also more expensive than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The American campus culture is truly amazing. I loved it!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything! I enjoyed the athlectic center with the gym, squash courts and different classes (yoga, spinning, HIT etc.). I also loved the Outing Club, and I went on more than 10 trips with them (hiking, biking etc.). I was also part of different social clubs at the law school, and they did things such as potlocks, quizzes, trips to other towns, parties etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join the Outing Club! It is great to do things outside Lexington.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Visit D.C, Charlottesville and Staunton. Take on trips with the Outing Club. Go to the parties. They begin early and end around midnight because everyone has to get up and study the day after.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was easy, but I was also very open-minded.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk with everyone if they seem interested! Be open and ask questions. Americans are open-minded and out-going, so they make you feel welcome in no time. However, the law students can be quite busy, so I enjoyed getting to know the undergrad students as well (on the trips with the Outing Club). They were less stressful.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Americans are loud in public. They almost yell when they are talking with each other. It was a bit difficult at first.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Americans and their openness. I felt so welcome.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. Be open and social. 2. Join different clubs and embrace all the options that the campus culture offers you. 3. Do the readings and participate in class. It will benefit you so much!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: As I already said, it is a lot of hard work! It is not an exchange stay with vacation vibes.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The academics, the campus culture and the people I met during my stay. I got some really good friends and I will miss them dearly.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The academics (It will be stressful, but you will get used to it. It was amazing to learn so much) and being in a small town.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
